questions.q: The word 'geography' comes from the Greek words 'geo' (earth) and 'graphos', which means ______.
questions.e: Geography literally means description of the earth.

questions.q: The term 'geography' was first used by the Greek scholar ______ (276-194 BC).
questions.e: Eratosthenes coined the term geography; he is also known for estimating the circumference of the earth.

questions.q: The approach in which one phenomenon, such as climate or landforms, is studied all over the world, introduced by Alexander von Humboldt, is called the ______ approach.
questions.e: Humboldt developed the systematic approach; Karl Ritter developed the regional approach, which divides the world into regions.

questions.t: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
questions.q: The scientist who provided evidence in 1920 that the universe is expanding was ______.
questions.e: Hubble showed that galaxies are moving farther apart, supporting the Big Bang (expanding universe) hypothesis.

questions.t: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
questions.q: According to the Big Bang theory, the universe began about how many billion years ago?
questions.e: Scientists believe the Big Bang took place about 13.7 billion years ago; the earth itself is about 4.6 billion years old.

questions.t: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
questions.q: The Nebular Hypothesis of the origin of the solar system was first given by the German philosopher ______ and was revised by the mathematician Laplace in 1796.
questions.e: Kant proposed that planets formed from a slowly rotating cloud of material (nebula) around a young sun; Laplace revised it in 1796.

questions.t: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
questions.q: The process by which gases were released from the interior of the earth, helping to form the early atmosphere, is called ______.
questions.e: During degassing, gases and water vapour escaped from the cooling earth's interior and evolved the present atmosphere.

questions.q: The mean thickness of the oceanic crust is about how many kilometres?
questions.e: The oceanic crust is about 5 km thick, while the continental crust is around 30 km thick and more under mountains.

questions.q: The upper portion of the mantle, the main source of magma that reaches the surface during volcanic eruptions, is called the ______.
questions.e: The asthenosphere extends up to about 400 km and is the source of magma for volcanoes.

questions.q: Which type of earthquake body waves can travel only through solid materials and not through liquids?
questions.e: S-waves cannot pass through liquids; their absence beyond a certain distance helped scientists infer a liquid outer core.

questions.q: The area on the earth's surface where neither P-waves nor S-waves of a particular earthquake are recorded is called the ______.
questions.e: The shadow zone lies between about 105 and 145 degrees from the epicentre and gives clues about the earth's interior.

questions.q: The continental drift theory was put forward in 1912 by the German meteorologist ______.
questions.e: Wegener argued that all continents once formed a single landmass that later broke up and drifted apart.

questions.q: According to Wegener, all the continents once formed a single super-continent called ______.
questions.e: Pangaea first split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwanaland in the south.

questions.q: The mega-ocean that surrounded the super-continent Pangaea was called ______.
questions.e: Panthalassa means 'all water'; it surrounded the single landmass Pangaea.

questions.q: The concept of sea floor spreading was put forward in 1961 by ______.
questions.e: Hess argued that new crust forms at mid-oceanic ridges as magma rises, pushing the ocean floor apart.

questions.q: Before the Indian plate collided with the Asian plate, the two were separated by the ______ Sea.
questions.e: As the Indian plate moved north, the Tethys Sea closed and its sediments were folded to form the Himalayas.

questions.q: According to the theory of plate tectonics, the lithosphere is broken into a number of large and small plates that move relative to one another.
p: (a) How many major plates are there?
(b) A boundary where plates move apart and new crust is formed is called a ______ boundary.
divergent|constructive|spreading
(c) A boundary where plates slide past each other horizontally, so crust is neither created nor destroyed, is called a ______ boundary.
transform|conservative
questions.e: There are seven major plates; at divergent boundaries new crust is formed, and at transform boundaries plates slide past each other.

questions.q: Which gas makes up about 78 per cent of the atmosphere by volume?
questions.e: Nitrogen forms about 78 per cent and oxygen about 21 per cent of dry air.

questions.q: The lowermost layer of the atmosphere, in which all weather changes take place, is the ______.
questions.e: The troposphere contains dust and water vapour, so clouds, rain and storms occur in it.

questions.q: The ozone layer, which absorbs ultraviolet radiation from the sun, lies mainly in the ______.
questions.e: The ozone layer in the stratosphere shields life on earth from harmful ultraviolet rays.

questions.q: The average height of the troposphere at the equator is about how many kilometres?
questions.e: The troposphere is about 18 km high at the equator and about 8 km at the poles, because strong convection at the equator carries heat higher.

questions.q: The atmosphere is divided into layers based on temperature.
p: (a) In the troposphere, temperature falls by 1 degree Celsius for every how many metres of height (normal lapse rate)?
m
(b) Which layer lies above the stratosphere and extends up to about 80 km?
mesosphere
(c) Which gas, about 0.04 per cent of the air, is transparent to incoming solar radiation but absorbs outgoing terrestrial radiation?
carbon dioxide|CO2
questions.e: The normal lapse rate is 1 degree C per 165 m; the mesosphere extends to about 80 km; carbon dioxide traps outgoing heat and is a greenhouse gas.

questions.t: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
questions.q: The energy received by the earth's surface from the sun in the form of short waves is called ______.
questions.e: Insolation means incoming solar radiation; the earth gives out terrestrial radiation as long waves.

questions.t: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
questions.q: On 4 July the earth is farthest from the sun. This position is called ______.
questions.e: At aphelion (4 July) the earth is about 152 million km from the sun; at perihelion (3 January) it is nearest.

questions.t: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
questions.q: Normally temperature decreases with height. When temperature increases with height instead, the condition is called ______.
questions.e: Inversion occurs on long, clear winter nights with still air, when the ground and the air close to it cool quickly.

questions.t: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature
questions.q: Of 100 units of insolation reaching the top of the atmosphere, how many units are reflected back to space before reaching the earth's surface (the earth's albedo)?
questions.e: About 35 units are reflected back to space by clouds, ice and the atmosphere; this reflected amount is the albedo of the earth.

questions.q: When the sun, the moon and the earth are in a straight line, the height of the tide is higher than normal. Such tides are called ______ tides.
questions.e: Spring tides occur at new moon and full moon, when the pull of the sun and moon act together.

questions.q: When the sun and the moon are at right angles to each other, the tides are lower than normal. These are called ______ tides.
questions.e: Neap tides occur about seven days after spring tides, when the pulls of the sun and moon partly cancel each other.

questions.q: Which cold ocean current flows northward along the west coast of South America?
questions.e: The cold Humboldt (Peruvian) current flows along the coasts of Chile and Peru; the Benguela flows off south-west Africa.

questions.q: The highest point of a wave is called the ______.
questions.e: The crest is the highest point and the trough the lowest point of a wave; wave height is the distance between them.

questions.q: With an area of about 3.28 million sq km, India's rank among the countries of the world by area is ______. (Write the number.)
questions.e: India is the seventh largest country in the world, covering about 2.4 per cent of the world's land area.

questions.q: India extends from about 68 degrees 7 minutes E to 97 degrees 25 minutes E longitude, so local time varies across the country.
p: (a) The Standard Meridian of India is 82 degrees 30 minutes E. Write this in decimal degrees.
°E
(b) The Standard Meridian passes through Mirzapur in which state?
Uttar Pradesh|UP
(c) Roughly how many hours is the difference in local time between the eastern and western ends of India?
hours
questions.e: 82 degrees 30 minutes = 82.5 degrees E, passing through Mirzapur (UP); a longitudinal extent of about 30 degrees gives a time difference of nearly two hours.

questions.q: Which Indian state shares international borders with Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh?
questions.e: West Bengal borders Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh; Sikkim borders Nepal, Bhutan and China but not Bangladesh.

questions.q: The highest peak of peninsular India, located in the Anaimalai hills, is ______.
questions.e: Anaimudi (2,695 m) in the Anaimalai hills of the Western Ghats is the highest peak of the peninsular plateau.

questions.q: The group of coral islands of India in the Arabian Sea is ______.
questions.e: Lakshadweep consists of small coral islands off the Kerala coast; the Andaman and Nicobar islands lie in the Bay of Bengal.

questions.q: The Mizo hills, part of the Purvachal ranges in north-east India, are also known as the ______ hills.
questions.e: The Purvachal includes the Patkai Bum, Naga hills, Manipur hills and the Mizo or Lushai hills.

questions.q: Longitudinal valleys lying between the Lesser Himalaya and the Shiwaliks, such as Dehra Dun, are known as ______.
questions.e: Duns are flat longitudinal valleys between the Himachal and the Shiwalik ranges, like Dehra Dun, Kotli Dun and Patli Dun.

questions.q: Which river has the largest river basin in India?
questions.e: The Ganga basin is the largest in India; the Godavari basin is the largest of the peninsular rivers.

questions.q: In Tibet, the Brahmaputra is known as the ______.
questions.e: The Brahmaputra flows east through Tibet as the Tsangpo, enters India as the Siang or Dihang, and is called the Jamuna in Bangladesh.

questions.q: Which west-flowing river flows through a rift valley between the Vindhya range in the north and the Satpura range in the south?
questions.e: The Narmada rises on the Amarkantak plateau and flows west in a rift valley, forming an estuary rather than a delta.

questions.q: The Ganga is the most important river of India in terms of its basin and cultural significance.
p: (a) The Ganga rises in the Gangotri glacier near Gaumukh in which district of Uttarakhand?
Uttarkashi
(b) At which place do the Alaknanda and the Bhagirathi meet to form the Ganga?
Devprayag|Devaprayag|Dev Prayag
(c) The delta formed by the Ganga and the Brahmaputra, the largest in the world, is called the ______ delta.
Sundarbans|Sundarban|Sunderbans|Sunderban
questions.e: The Ganga rises at Gaumukh in Uttarkashi district, is formed at Devprayag, and with the Brahmaputra forms the Sundarbans delta.

questions.q: Under the Indus Water Treaty (1960), India can use only how many per cent of the total discharge of the Indus river system?
questions.e: India uses about 20 per cent of the Indus system's water, mainly for irrigation in Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan.

questions.q: The place in Meghalaya that receives the highest average annual rainfall in the world is ______.
questions.e: Mawsynram, in the Khasi hills, receives the highest average annual rainfall in the world.

questions.q: Pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and coastal Karnataka that help the early ripening of mangoes are called ______.
questions.e: Mango showers occur towards the end of summer; blossom showers help coffee flowers bloom in Kerala and Karnataka.

questions.q: The strong, hot, dry winds that blow in the afternoon over north and north-west India in May and June are called ______.
questions.e: The loo is a hot, dry local wind of the Indian summer; exposure to it can cause heatstroke.

questions.q: Different weather systems bring rain to different parts of India in different seasons.
p: (a) Name the weather systems that enter north-west India from the west in winter and bring rain to Punjab and Haryana.
western disturbances|western disturbance|western cyclones|temperate cyclones
(b) What are the dreaded evening thunderstorms of Bengal and Assam in the hot season called?
kalbaisakhi|kalbaishakhi|norwesters|nor westers|nor'westers
(c) By which date in June does the south-west monsoon normally reach the Kerala coast?
questions.e: Western disturbances give winter rain in the north-west; kalbaisakhi storms hit Bengal in summer; the monsoon usually reaches Kerala by 1 June.

questions.q: Ebony, mahogany and rosewood are important trees of ______ forests.
questions.a: tropical evergreen|evergreen|tropical evergreen forests|tropical evergreen forest
questions.e: Tropical evergreen forests grow in areas with over 200 cm of rainfall, such as the Western Ghats.

questions.q: Teak and sal are important trees of which type of forests, also called monsoon forests?
questions.a: tropical deciduous|deciduous|tropical deciduous forests|tropical deciduous forest
questions.e: Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests are the most widespread in India and shed their leaves in the dry season.

questions.q: India's National Forest Policy aims to bring how many per cent of the country's geographical area under forest cover?
questions.e: The National Forest Policy aims at having one-third (33 per cent) of the geographical area under forest.

questions.q: Which was the first biosphere reserve set up in India, in 1986?
questions.e: The Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve (1986) covers parts of Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Karnataka.

questions.q: The school of thought which holds that human beings are controlled by their natural environment is called environmental ______.
questions.e: Environmental determinism sees nature as all-powerful; early humans adapted to and depended on nature.

questions.q: The view that people use the opportunities provided by nature to create possibilities with the help of technology is called ______.
questions.e: In possibilism, nature provides opportunities and humans make use of them, creating a humanised landscape.

questions.q: The concept of neo-determinism, also called 'stop and go determinism', was put forward by ______.
questions.e: Griffith Taylor argued for a middle path: humans can conquer nature by obeying it, like following traffic lights.

questions.q: Who defined human geography as 'the synthetic study of relationship between human societies and earth's surface'?
questions.e: Ratzel's definition stresses synthesis, the joining of studies of society and of the earth's surface.

questions.q: The number of people living per unit area of land is called ______.
questions.e: Population density = population divided by area, usually given as persons per sq km.

questions.q: The theory that explains how a region's population changes from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates as it develops is called the ______.
questions.a: demographic transition theory|demographic transition|demographic transition model
questions.e: Demographic transition theory describes how a society moves from rural, agrarian and illiterate to urban, industrial and literate, with falling birth and death rates.

questions.q: Which economist's population theory stated that the number of people would increase faster than the food supply?
questions.e: Malthus argued that population grows faster than food supply, leading to famine, disease and war that check population.

questions.q: The increase in the population of an area due only to the difference between births and deaths is called ______.
questions.a: natural growth|natural increase|natural growth of population
questions.e: Natural growth = births minus deaths; actual growth also includes in-migration minus out-migration.

questions.q: A district has a crude birth rate of 30 per thousand and a crude death rate of 10 per thousand. Migration is negligible.
p: (a) What is its natural growth rate per thousand?
per thousand
(b) Express this growth rate as a percentage.
(c) If the population is 50,00,000, by how many people will it grow in one year?
questions.e: Natural growth = 30 - 10 = 20 per thousand = 2 per cent; 2 per cent of 50,00,000 = 1,00,000 people.

questions.q: Which organisation has published the Human Development Report every year since 1990?
questions.a: UNDP|United Nations Development Programme|United Nations Development Program
questions.e: The UNDP publishes the Human Development Report, which ranks countries by their Human Development Index.

questions.q: The concept of human development was introduced by the Pakistani economist ______.
questions.a: Mahbub-ul-Haq|Mahbub ul Haq|Mahbubul Haq|Dr Mahbub ul Haq
questions.e: Mahbub-ul-Haq described human development as development that enlarges people's choices and improves their lives.

questions.q: Which Nobel laureate economist saw an increase in freedom (or decrease in unfreedom) as the main objective of development?
questions.e: Amartya Sen argued that development means increasing people's freedoms, which depend on social and political institutions.

questions.q: The four pillars of human development are equity, sustainability, productivity and ______.
questions.e: Empowerment means having the power to make choices, which comes from increasing freedom and capability.

questions.q: Shifting cultivation is called ______ in north-eastern India.
questions.e: Shifting cultivation is called jhuming in north-east India, milpa in Central America and ladang in Malaysia.

questions.q: The seasonal movement of herders and their animals, such as to mountain pastures in summer and to lower areas in winter, is called ______.
questions.e: In transhumance, herders like the Gujjars and Bakarwals move between plains and mountain pastures with the seasons.

questions.q: Commercial grain farming in North America is practised in the temperate grasslands called the ______.
questions.e: Wheat is the main crop of the prairies; the steppes of Eurasia and pampas of Argentina are other temperate grasslands.

questions.q: The collective farming system introduced in the former Soviet Union was called ______.
questions.e: In a kolkhoz, farmers pooled their land, livestock and labour, keeping small plots for their own needs.

questions.q: Plantation agriculture was introduced by Europeans in their colonies in the tropics.
p: (a) Which European people set up large tea gardens in India and Sri Lanka?
British|Britain|English|England
(b) Which European people established sugarcane plantations in Indonesia (Java)?
Dutch|Netherlands|Holland
(c) Which European people set up coffee and cocoa plantations in West Africa?
French|France
questions.e: The British set up tea gardens in India and Sri Lanka, the Dutch sugarcane in Java and the French coffee and cocoa in West Africa.

questions.q: The cotton textile industry, which uses raw material from farms, is an example of a(n) ______ industry.
questions.e: Agro-based industries process farm products such as cotton, sugarcane and fruits into finished goods.

questions.q: Industries that can be located in a wide variety of places, because they do not depend on a specific raw material, are called ______ industries.
questions.e: Footloose industries depend on component parts that can be got anywhere and mainly need good road access.

questions.q: The well-known high-tech industrial region near San Francisco in the USA is called ______.
questions.e: High-tech industries cluster in technopoles such as Silicon Valley near San Francisco and Silicon Forest near Seattle.

questions.q: An industry owned jointly by the government and private individuals or companies is said to be in the ______ sector.
questions.e: By ownership, industries are public sector, private sector or joint sector.

questions.q: Activities centred on the research, development and handling of knowledge and information are called ______ activities.
questions.e: Quaternary activities include research, information technology and education, and form an advanced part of the service sector.

questions.q: Services of the highest-level decision-makers and policy makers, sometimes called 'gold collar' professions, belong to ______ activities.
questions.e: Quinary activities include senior business executives, government officials, research scientists and financial and legal consultants.

questions.q: Outsourcing that involves highly skilled workers doing research, analysis and information-driven work is called ______.
questions.e: KPO requires specialised knowledge, unlike BPO, which handles routine business processes like call centres.

questions.q: When patients from abroad travel to India for treatment such as surgery, it is called ______ tourism.
questions.e: India has become a leading country for medical tourism because of good hospitals and lower costs.

questions.q: The longest double-tracked, electrified trans-continental railway in the world, running across Russia, is the ______.
questions.e: The Trans-Siberian Railway, about 9,332 km long, links the European part of Russia with its Pacific coast.

questions.q: The Trans-Siberian Railway runs from St Petersburg in the west to ______ on the Pacific coast in the east.
questions.e: It runs from St Petersburg to Vladivostok, passing through Moscow, Novosibirsk, Irkutsk and other cities.

questions.q: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, links the Mediterranean Sea with the ______.
questions.e: The Suez Canal runs from Port Said to Port Suez and gives Europe a shorter sea route to the Indian Ocean.

questions.q: The Panama Canal, joining the Atlantic and the Pacific Oceans, was opened in ______.
questions.e: The Panama Canal was built by the USA and opened in 1914; it shortened the sea route between New York and San Francisco.

questions.q: The famous 'Big Inch' pipeline in the USA carries petroleum from the oil wells of the Gulf of Mexico to the ______.
questions.a: north-eastern states of the USA|north-eastern USA|north-east USA|north-eastern states|northeastern states
questions.e: The Big Inch pipeline moves petroleum overland from the Gulf of Mexico oil fields to the industrial north-eastern states.

questions.q: The World Trade Organisation came into existence on 1 January ______.
questions.e: The WTO was set up in 1995 to frame rules for global trade and settle trade disputes between member nations.

questions.q: The WTO replaced which earlier arrangement, set up in 1948 to liberalise world trade?
questions.a: GATT|General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade
questions.e: GATT was formed in 1948 to reduce tariffs; it was transformed into the WTO in 1995.

questions.q: The difference between the value of a country's imports and exports of goods and services is called its ______.
questions.e: If imports exceed exports the balance of trade is negative (unfavourable); if exports exceed imports it is positive.

questions.q: In a year, Country P exports goods worth ₹500 crore and imports goods worth ₹650 crore.
p: (a) Calculate its balance of trade in ₹ crore (use a minus sign for a deficit).
(b) Is this balance of trade favourable or unfavourable?
unfavourable|unfavorable|negative|deficit
(c) Trade between only two countries, under an agreement between them, is called ______ trade.
bilateral
questions.e: 500 - 650 = -150 crore, an unfavourable (negative) balance of trade; trade between two countries is bilateral trade.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: According to Census 2011, the most populous state of India is ______.
questions.e: Uttar Pradesh had about 16 per cent of India's population in 2011, followed by Maharashtra and Bihar.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: According to Census 2011, the density of population of India was how many persons per sq km?
questions.e: India's population density rose to 382 persons per sq km in 2011, with Bihar the highest among states.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: According to Census 2011, which state has the highest sex ratio in India?
questions.e: Kerala had a sex ratio of 1,084 females per 1,000 males, the highest among Indian states.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: According to Census 2011, which state has the lowest density of population in India (about 17 persons per sq km)?
questions.e: Rugged terrain and unfavourable climate give Arunachal Pradesh the lowest population density of 17 persons per sq km.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: The period 1921-1951 in India's population history is referred to as the period of ______ population growth.
questions.e: 1901-1921 was a period of stagnant growth, 1921-1951 steady growth, and 1951-1981 a population explosion.

questions.q: Rice, sown with the onset of the south-west monsoon, is mainly a ______ crop in most parts of India.
questions.e: Kharif crops are sown with the south-west monsoon; rabi crops like wheat are sown in winter.

questions.q: The short summer cropping season after the rabi harvest, in which crops like watermelons and cucumbers are grown, is called ______.
questions.e: Zaid is a short-duration summer season, mostly on irrigated land, for vegetables, fruits and fodder crops.

questions.q: A farmer's net sown area is 100 hectares and gross cropped area is 150 hectares. Using cropping intensity = (GCA / NSA) x 100, find the cropping intensity.
questions.e: Cropping intensity = 150 / 100 x 100 = 150 per cent, meaning part of the land is cropped twice a year.

questions.q: Land-use records in India classify land into several categories.
p: (a) Land left uncultivated for one year or less is called ______.
current fallow|current fallows
(b) Land left uncultivated for more than five years is called ______.
culturable waste land|culturable waste|culturable wasteland
(c) Which state is the leading producer of tea in India?
Assam
questions.e: Current fallow is left uncultivated for up to a year, culturable waste land for over five years; Assam is India's largest tea producer.

questions.q: High-yielding varieties of wheat introduced in India during the Green Revolution came from ______.
questions.e: HYV wheat seeds came from Mexico and HYV rice from the Philippines (IRRI) in the mid-1960s.

questions.q: Which iron ore has the highest iron content, up to about 70 per cent?
questions.e: Magnetite is the finest iron ore with up to 70 per cent iron; haematite has 50-60 per cent.

questions.q: The Jharia coalfield, important for coking coal, is in which state?
questions.e: Jharia in Jharkhand is the largest coalfield of the Damodar valley, followed by Raniganj in West Bengal.

questions.q: The monazite sands of coastal Kerala are an important source of ______, used for atomic energy.
questions.e: Thorium is obtained mainly from monazite in the beach sands of Kerala; uranium comes mostly from Jharkhand.

questions.q: The oldest oil field of India, in Assam, is ______.
questions.e: Assam is the oldest oil-producing state; Digboi, Naharkatiya and Moran are its important oil fields.

questions.q: India is developing both conventional and non-conventional sources of energy.
p: (a) The geothermal energy project at Manikaran is in which state?
Himachal Pradesh|HP
(b) The Gulf of Khambhat, with great potential for tidal energy, is in which state?
Gujarat
(c) The Tarapur atomic power station is in which state?
Maharashtra
questions.e: Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh) has a geothermal plant, the Gulf of Khambhat (Gujarat) has tidal potential and Tarapur (Maharashtra) has an atomic power station.

questions.q: Who defined human geography as "the study of the changing relationship between the unresting man and the unstable earth"?
questions.a: Ellen C. Semple|Ellen Semple|Semple|Ellen Churchill Semple
questions.e: Ellen C. Semple stressed the dynamic nature of the relationship between humans and the earth.

questions.q: Population geography is closely linked with which sister discipline in the social sciences?
questions.e: Demography is the study of population size, composition and change.

questions.q: The approach in human geography that emerged in the 1990s, questioning grand generalisations and universal theories, is ______.
questions.e: It stressed the importance of understanding each local context.

questions.q: Electoral geography is closely linked with which sister discipline, the study of elections?
questions.e: Electoral geography studies the spatial patterns of voting and elections.

questions.q: Medical geography is closely linked with which sister discipline?
questions.e: Epidemiology is the study of the spread and control of diseases.

questions.q: When people with a low level of technology depend directly on nature and adapt to its dictates, NCERT describes this as the ______ of humans.
questions.e: Over time, with better technology, nature is humanised and bears the imprint of human endeavour.

questions.q: The school of thought in human geography that used Marxian theory to explain the basic causes of poverty, deprivation and social inequality is the ______ school.
questions.e: It emerged in the 1970s along with the humanistic and behavioural schools.

questions.q: The French geographer whose view of human geography stressed "a more synthetic knowledge of the physical laws governing our earth" was Paul ______.
questions.a: Vidal de la Blache|Vidal de la Blanche|de la Blache
questions.e: Paul Vidal de la Blache is associated with the possibilist view.

questions.q: In NCERT's example of the naturalisation of humans, Benda lives in the wilds of the ______ area of central India.
questions.e: His tribe depends directly on the forest for food, medicine and shelter.

questions.q: The approach in human geography in the inter-war period of the 1930s, which aimed to identify how and why one region differs from another, was ______.
questions.e: The focus was on identifying the uniqueness of any region.

questions.q: The approach of the late 1950s and 1960s, marked by the use of computers and statistical tools and called the quantitative revolution, was ______.
questions.e: Laws of physics were often applied to map and analyse human phenomena.

questions.q: Which school of human geography laid great emphasis on lived experience and on the perception of space by social categories?
questions.e: The behavioural school considered how ethnicity, race and religion shape the perception of space.

questions.q: NCERT lists the broad stages through which human geography developed as an academic field.
p: (a) Which approach was used in the early colonial period, when imperial and trade interests prompted the discovery of new areas?
exploration and description|exploration
(b) Which approach followed in the later colonial period, describing all aspects of a region in detail?
regional analysis|regional
questions.e: Exploration and description was followed by regional analysis, then areal differentiation (1930s) and spatial organisation (1950s-1960s).

questions.q: The three components of population change are births, deaths and ______.
questions.e: Migration changes the population of both the place of origin and the place of destination.

questions.q: The place to which a migrant moves is called the place of ______.
questions.e: The place from which people move is the place of origin.

questions.q: Unemployment, poor living conditions, political turmoil and epidemics are ______ factors that make people leave a place.
questions.e: Pull factors such as better jobs and living conditions attract people to a place.

questions.q: In the first stage of the demographic transition, both fertility and mortality are ______.
questions.e: Population growth is slow because high deaths offset high births.

questions.q: About 90 per cent of the world's population lives in about what percentage of its land area?
questions.e: The distribution of the world's population is extremely uneven.

questions.q: The 10 most populous countries of the world together contribute about what percentage of the world's population?
questions.e: Of these 10 countries, 6 are located in Asia.

questions.q: Of the 10 most populous countries of the world, how many are located in Asia?
questions.e: Asia has many people and a high population density.

questions.q: The crude birth rate is the number of live births in a year per how many people?
questions.e: The crude birth rate and the crude death rate are both expressed per thousand of population.

questions.q: When the birth rate falls below the death rate, population growth is said to be ______.
questions.e: Population growth is positive when the birth rate is higher than the death rate.

questions.q: The mineral-rich ______ Zambia copper belt in Africa is an example of mineral deposits attracting people.
questions.e: Areas with mineral deposits attract industries, and mining and industrial activities create jobs.

questions.q: In which stage of the demographic transition does fertility remain high while mortality falls, leading to a huge increase in population?
questions.e: Improved health and sanitation reduce mortality while fertility declines only later.

questions.q: A country has a population of 50 million and an area of 250,000 sq km.
p: (a) What is its density of population, in persons per sq km?
persons per sq km
(b) If its population grows to 60 million on the same area, what will the density be?
persons per sq km
questions.e: Density = population / area: 50,000,000 / 250,000 = 200, and 60,000,000 / 250,000 = 240 persons per sq km.

questions.q: Growth is quantitative and value-neutral, while development means a ______ change which is always value-positive.
questions.e: Development occurs when there is a positive change in quality.

questions.q: In the Human Development Index, health is assessed using life ______ at birth.
questions.e: A higher life expectancy means people have a greater chance of living longer and healthier lives.

questions.q: The Human Development Index score of a country lies between ______ and 1.
questions.e: The closer the score is to 1, the greater the level of human development.

questions.q: Which country officially uses Gross National Happiness (GNH) as the measure of its progress?
questions.e: Bhutan is the only country in the world to do so officially.

questions.q: The pillar of human development that means making equal access to opportunities available to everybody is ______.
questions.e: Opportunities should be available irrespective of gender, race, income and, in India, caste.

questions.q: The pillar of human development that means continuity in the availability of opportunities, for present and future generations, is ______.
questions.e: Resources must be used in a way that does not restrict the choices of future generations.

questions.q: The oldest approach to human development, which links it with income, is the ______ approach.
questions.e: The idea is that the level of income reflects the level of freedom an individual enjoys.

questions.q: The basic needs approach to human development was initially proposed by the ______.
questions.e: It identified six basic needs: health, education, food, water supply, sanitation and housing.

questions.q: How many basic needs were identified in the basic needs approach?
questions.e: They are health, education, food, water supply, sanitation and housing.

questions.q: The approach that sees human beings as beneficiaries of development and argues for higher government spending on education, health and amenities is the ______ approach.
questions.e: In this approach the government is responsible for increasing levels of human development.

questions.q: The approach associated with Prof. Amartya Sen, which focuses on building human capabilities in health, education and access to resources, is the ______ approach.
questions.e: Building capabilities is seen as the key to increasing human development.

questions.q: The Human Poverty Index is related to the HDI and measures the ______ in human development.
questions.e: The HDI measures attainments, while the Human Poverty Index measures the shortfall.

questions.q: The HDI ranks countries on the basis of performance in health, education and access to resources.
p: (a) Besides the gross enrolment ratio, which rate is used to measure education?
adult literacy rate|literacy rate|adult literacy|literacy
(b) In terms of what kind of power is access to resources measured?
purchasing power|purchasing
questions.e: Education is measured by the adult literacy rate and the gross enrolment ratio; access to resources is measured by purchasing power in US dollars.

questions.q: Primary activities depend directly on the ______.
questions.e: They make use of earth resources such as land, water, vegetation and minerals.

questions.q: Shifting (slash and burn) cultivation is called ______ in Mexico and Central America.
questions.e: It is called jhuming in north-eastern India and ladang in Indonesia and Malaysia.

questions.q: The cultivation of grapes, a speciality of the Mediterranean region, is called ______.
questions.e: Best quality wines of the world are produced from high quality grapes grown in this region.

questions.q: Shifting cultivation is called ______ in Indonesia and Malaysia.
questions.e: Each name refers to the same practice of clearing and burning vegetation and moving on when the soil loses fertility.

questions.q: In pastoral nomadism, the most important animal in the Arctic and sub-Arctic areas is the ______.
questions.e: Yaks and llamas are reared in the mountains of Tibet and the Andes.

questions.q: In which country has the co-operative farming movement been so successful that practically every farmer is a member of a co-operative?
questions.e: Co-operative farming is also successful in the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden and Italy.

questions.q: Farming in which farmers specialise only in vegetables, with farms located within the distance a truck can cover overnight, is called ______ farming.
questions.e: It is a form of market gardening and horticulture serving urban markets.

questions.q: The temperate grasslands of Argentina, an area of extensive commercial grain farming, are called the ______.
questions.e: Other such grasslands are the Prairies, the Steppes, the Velds and the Downs.

questions.q: The rearing of livestock, especially poultry and cattle, in stalls and pens with manufactured feed and careful health care is called ______ farming.
questions.e: It is practised in Western Europe and North America.

questions.q: Commercial livestock rearing on large, permanent, fenced farms is called ______.
questions.e: Ranching is practised in New Zealand, Australia, Argentina, Uruguay and the USA.

questions.q: In plantation agriculture, the French established cocoa and coffee plantations in ______ Africa.
questions.e: The British set up tea gardens in India and Sri Lanka and rubber plantations in Malaysia.

questions.q: There are two main methods of mining.
p: (a) Mining of minerals lying close to the surface is called surface mining or ______ mining.
open-cast|open cast|opencast
(b) Underground mining, used when the ore lies deep below the surface, is also called the ______ method.
shaft|shafts
questions.e: Open-cast mining is the easiest and cheapest; the shaft method needs lifts, drills, haulage vehicles and ventilation.

questions.q: The word manufacturing literally means to make by ______.
questions.e: It now includes goods made by machines in factories.

questions.q: Industries owned and managed by governments are ______ sector industries.
questions.e: Private sector industries are owned by individual investors.

questions.q: The smallest manufacturing units, run by artisans with the help of family members using local raw materials, are ______ industries.
questions.e: Their products are usually consumed in the household or sold in local markets.

questions.q: Industries whose products are used to make other goods, such as iron and steel, are called ______ industries.
questions.e: Iron and steel is a basic industry because many other industries depend on it.

questions.q: Industries producing goods such as tea, biscuits and soaps that are consumed directly by people are called ______ industries.
questions.e: Their products are bought directly by consumers.

questions.q: Industries that use raw materials such as timber, bamboo and grass, for example paper and furniture, are ______ industries.
questions.e: Forests provide many major and minor products used as raw materials.

questions.q: Mineral-based industries that use metals containing iron are called ______ industries.
questions.e: Aluminium, copper and jewellery industries, which use other metals, are non-ferrous.

questions.q: Industries such as petrochemicals, plastics and fertilisers, which use natural chemical minerals, are ______ industries.
questions.e: Salt and potash are among the natural chemical minerals used.

questions.q: The latest generation of manufacturing, based on intensive research and development (R&D), is called ______ industry.
questions.e: A high proportion of its workforce consists of professional (white collar) workers.

questions.q: Regionally concentrated, self-sustained and highly specialised high-tech industrial areas are called ______.
questions.e: Silicon Valley near San Francisco is an example.

questions.q: Industries using weight-losing raw materials, such as ore smelting, are usually located close to the ______.
questions.a: raw material|raw materials|source of raw material|sources of raw material
questions.e: Locating near the raw material reduces transport costs.

questions.q: Industries are classified by size, based on capital invested, number of workers and volume of production.
p: (a) Which industries use local raw material, simple power-driven machines and semi-skilled labour?
small-scale|small scale|smallscale
(b) Which industries need a large market, varied raw materials, enormous energy, skilled workers and advanced technology?
large-scale|large scale|largescale
questions.e: Small-scale industries use simple power-driven machines, while large-scale industries involve assembly-line mass production.

questions.q: Trade, transport, communication and services are ______ activities.
questions.e: Tertiary activities provide services rather than producing goods.

questions.q: The business of selling goods directly to consumers is called ______ trading.
questions.e: Most retail trading takes place in fixed establishments or stores.

questions.q: Markets held at regular intervals in rural areas, such as weekly or bi-weekly, are called ______ markets.
questions.e: People from surrounding areas meet in them to buy and sell.

questions.q: Trade carried out through numerous intermediary merchants and supply houses, rather than with consumers, is called ______ trade.
questions.e: Wholesale merchants often extend credit to retail stores.

questions.q: Mail order, telephone marketing and automatic vending machines are examples of ______ retail trading.
questions.e: Store-based retailing includes consumer co-operatives, departmental stores and chain stores.

questions.q: Which tertiary activity has become the world's single largest in total registered jobs?
questions.e: Tourism also accounts for a large share of total revenue.

questions.q: Outsourcing of business work such as call centres to companies in other countries is known as ______.
questions.e: Business process outsourcing involves less skilled work than knowledge processing outsourcing.

questions.q: Quaternary activities centre around the collection, production and dissemination of ______.
questions.e: They include research, development and specialised knowledge-based services.

questions.q: The gap between people who have access to information and communication technology and those who do not is called the ______.
questions.e: Opportunities from ICT are unevenly distributed across countries and within them.

questions.q: The warm places around the ______ coast in Europe and the west coast of India are among the most popular tourist destinations.
questions.e: Climate is one of the main tourist attractions.

questions.q: When outsourcing involves transferring work to overseas locations, it is described by the term ______.
questions.e: Outsourcing is giving work to an outside agency to improve efficiency and reduce costs.

questions.q: Store-based retail trading takes several forms.
p: (a) What are large retail units with several departments under one roof called?
departmental stores|departmental store|department stores|department store|departmental
(b) What are stores of one company with many outlets, able to buy merchandise most economically, called?
chain stores|chain store|chain
questions.e: Departmental stores delegate purchasing to departmental heads; chain stores can buy directly from manufacturers and employ highly skilled specialists.

questions.q: The fastest mode of transport is ______ transport.
questions.e: No place in the world is now more than about 35 hours away by air.

questions.q: The cheapest mode of transport for heavy and bulky goods over long distances is ______ transport.
questions.e: Water transport needs no route construction, and the energy cost is low.

questions.q: The Trans-Canadian Railway runs from Halifax in the east to ______ on the Pacific coast.
questions.e: It passes through Montreal, Ottawa, Winnipeg and Calgary.

questions.q: The Australian Trans-Continental Railway runs across the south of the continent from Perth on the west coast to ______ on the east coast.
questions.e: It crosses the Nullarbor Plain.

questions.q: The Orient Express ran from Paris to ______.
questions.e: It passed through Strasbourg, Munich, Vienna, Budapest and Belgrade.

questions.q: The Union and Pacific Railway connects New York on the Atlantic coast with ______ on the Pacific coast.
questions.e: It passes through Cleveland, Chicago, Omaha, Evans, Ogden and Sacramento.

questions.q: The world's most heavily used inland waterway, navigable for about 700 km from Rotterdam to Basel in Switzerland, is the ______.
questions.e: It flows through a rich coalfield and the industrial area of the Ruhr.

questions.q: The Northern Atlantic Sea Route, linking north-eastern USA and north-western Europe, is also called the ______.
questions.a: Big Trunk Route|Big Trunk|Big Trunk Road
questions.e: It carries about one-fourth of the world's foreign trade.

questions.q: The Volga, one of the most important inland waterways of Russia, drains into the ______ Sea.
questions.e: The Volga-Don Canal connects it with the Don river.

questions.q: The Stuart Highway in Australia connects Darwin on the north coast with ______, via Alice Springs.
questions.e: It also passes through Tennant Creek.

questions.q: Two shipping canals serve as gateways of commerce for the eastern and western worlds.
p: (a) How many locks does the Panama Canal have?
(b) What is the approximate length of the Suez Canal?
km
questions.e: The Panama Canal has a six-lock system; the Suez Canal is about 160 km long and 11 to 15 m deep.

questions.q: Trade carried out by two countries with each other, according to an agreement, is called ______ trade.
questions.e: The countries agree to trade specified commodities with each other.

questions.q: Trade conducted by a country with many trading partners is called ______ trade.
questions.e: The same country can trade with a number of other countries.

questions.q: The ancient long-distance trade route that connected Rome to China was the ______.
questions.e: It was about 6,000 km long and carried Chinese silk, Roman wool and precious metals.

questions.q: Selling a commodity in another country at a price lower than its cost of production in the home country is called ______.
questions.e: Countries need to be careful about dumped goods, as they can harm local producers.

questions.q: Opening up economies for trading by bringing down trade barriers such as tariffs is called free trade or trade ______.
questions.e: Free trade allows goods and services from everywhere to compete with domestic products.

questions.q: The headquarters of the World Trade Organisation is in ______.
questions.e: The WTO sets the rules for the global trading system.

questions.q: The headquarters of OPEC (Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries) is in ______.
questions.e: OPEC aims to coordinate and unify petroleum policies.

questions.q: The actual tonnage of goods traded makes up the ______ of trade.
questions.e: Services cannot be measured in tonnage, so the total value of goods and services traded is used as the volume of trade.

questions.q: The headquarters of ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations) is in ______.
questions.e: ASEAN aims to accelerate economic growth and cultural development.

questions.q: The headquarters of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) is in ______.
questions.e: Minsk is in Belarus.

questions.q: The headquarters of the Latin American Integration Association (LAIA) is in ______.
questions.e: Montevideo is in Uruguay.

questions.q: The South Asian Free Trade Agreement (SAFTA) came into force in January of which year?
questions.e: SAFTA aims to reduce tariffs on intra-regional trade.

questions.q: Regional trade blocs have come up to encourage trade between countries with geographical proximity.
p: (a) In which city is the headquarters of the European Union?
Brussels
(b) In which year was ASEAN formed?
questions.e: The European Union is headquartered in Brussels, Belgium; ASEAN was formed in 1967.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: India accounts for about what percentage of the world's area?
questions.e: On this small share of the world's area India supports a very large share of the world's population.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: According to Census 2011, India's population accounts for about what percentage of the world's population?
questions.e: India's population as per Census 2011 was 1,210 million.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: The period 1901-1921 is described as a period of ______ or stationary phase of growth of India's population.
questions.e: Both birth and death rates were high, keeping growth very low.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: The period 1951-1981 is referred to as the period of population ______ in India.
questions.e: Mortality fell rapidly while fertility remained high.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: According to the Census of India, a main worker is a person who works for at least how many days in a year?
questions.e: 183 days is about six months; those who work for less are marginal workers.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: According to Census 2011, which state of India has the highest density of population?
questions.e: Bihar's density was over 1,100 persons per sq km in 2011.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: Hindi, Bengali and Marathi belong to which language family?
questions.e: The Indo-European (Aryan) family is spoken by the largest share of India's people.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: The ratio between the total population and the net cultivated area is called ______ density.
questions.e: Agricultural density is the total agricultural population divided by the net cultivable area.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: According to Grierson's Linguistic Survey of India (1903-1928), how many languages were there in India?
questions.e: The survey also recorded as many as 544 dialects.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: Santhali, Mundari and Ho belong to which language family?
questions.e: The Munda branch of the Austric family is spoken in Jharkhand and nearby areas.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: In which decade did India record a negative growth rate of population?
questions.e: Famines, epidemics and high mortality caused the population to fall slightly in 1911-1921.

questions.t: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
questions.q: Census 2011 gives the distribution of India's population by state and by work.
p: (a) Which state is the second most populous after Uttar Pradesh?
Maharashtra
(b) What are people who work for less than 183 days in a year called?
marginal workers|marginal worker|marginal
questions.e: Uttar Pradesh is followed by Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh; those who work less than 183 days a year are marginal workers.

questions.q: Tea plantation in India was started in 1840 in the ______ valley of Assam.
questions.e: Tea is a plantation crop grown in humid, hilly areas.

questions.q: Wheat is mainly a ______ crop in India.
questions.e: Wheat is grown in winter and harvested in spring.

questions.q: Farming in areas with annual rainfall of less than 75 cm is called ______ farming.
questions.e: Drought-resistant crops such as ragi, bajra, moong and gram are grown.

questions.q: In West Bengal farmers grow three crops of rice called aus, aman and ______.
questions.e: These crops are grown in different seasons of the year.

questions.q: Gram and tur (arhar) are examples of ______ crops.
questions.e: Pulses are a rich source of protein and fix nitrogen in the soil.

questions.q: Which state produces about two-fifths of India's sugarcane?
questions.e: Sugarcane is grown widely in the plains of western and central Uttar Pradesh.

questions.q: The new agricultural strategy of the mid-1960s, based on high-yielding varieties of seeds, fertilisers and irrigation, led to the ______ Revolution.
questions.e: It was first adopted in irrigated areas such as Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.

questions.q: Which state alone produces more than half of India's jowar (sorghum)?
questions.e: Jowar is grown in central and southern India.

questions.q: The long-staple American cotton grown in the north-western parts of India is called ______.
questions.e: India grows both short-staple (Indian) and long-staple (American) cotton.

questions.q: Village pastures, community forests and ponds, owned by the state but used by all, are called ______ resources.
questions.e: They provide fodder, fuel and minor forest products, especially for the landless and poor.

questions.q: Tea is an important plantation crop of India.
p: (a) In which year was tea plantation started in Assam?
(b) Which hill district of West Bengal is a major tea-growing area?
Darjeeling
questions.e: Tea plantation began in the Brahmaputra valley of Assam in 1840; in West Bengal it is grown in Darjeeling, Jalpaiguri and Cooch Behar districts.

questions.q: Important deposits of lignite are found at ______ in Tamil Nadu.
questions.e: Lignite is a low grade brown coal used to generate electricity.

questions.q: Iron ore, manganese and chromite are ______ metallic minerals.
questions.e: Copper and bauxite are non-ferrous metallic minerals.

questions.q: The Khetri copper mines are in which state?
questions.e: Copper is also mined in Singhbhum (Jharkhand) and Balaghat (Madhya Pradesh).

questions.q: The Bailadila iron ore mines are in which state?
questions.e: Bailadila is in Dantewada district and produces high grade haematite.

questions.q: The Kudremukh iron ore deposits are in which state?
questions.e: Kudremukh is in the Western Ghats.

questions.q: Kalahandi and Sambalpur are leading bauxite-producing areas of ______, the largest producer of bauxite in India.
questions.e: Bauxite is the ore used in manufacturing aluminium.

questions.q: The offshore oil field of Mumbai High came into production in ______.
questions.e: It is one of India's most important oil fields.

questions.q: Which mineral, mined in Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan, is mainly used in the electrical and electronic industries?
questions.e: Mica can be split into very thin sheets that are tough and flexible.

questions.q: The most important ______ coalfields of India are located in the Damodar valley.
questions.e: Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro are important coalfields in this region.

questions.q: The Atomic Energy Institute at Trombay, set up in 1954, was renamed the ______ in 1967.
questions.a: Bhabha Atomic Research Centre|BARC|Bhabha Atomic Research Center
questions.e: The Atomic Energy Commission had been set up in 1948.

questions.q: The Rawatbhata nuclear power project is near ______ in Rajasthan.
questions.e: Other nuclear power projects include Tarapur, Kalpakkam, Narora, Kaiga and Kakrapara.

questions.q: Petroleum and natural gas are important energy resources.
p: (a) In which year was the Gas Authority of India Limited (GAIL) set up?
(b) In which state is the Ankleshwar oil field?
Gujarat
questions.e: GAIL was set up in 1984 to transport and market natural gas; Ankleshwar is one of the main oil fields of Gujarat.
